answer_text:
Let the field be arbitrary, and let \(J\) be the all-one square matrix of the same size as \(A\). Write

\[
J = \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T},
\]

where \(\mathbf{1}\) is the all-one column vector. Since \(\mathbf{1}\neq 0\) in any field, \(J\) has rank \(1\) (for \(n\ge 1\)).

For any two same-size matrices \(X,Y\), we have the rank subadditivity inequality

\[
\operatorname{rank}(X+Y)\le \operatorname{rank}(X)+\operatorname{rank}(Y),
\]

because the column space of \(X+Y\) is contained in the sum of the column spaces of \(X\) and \(Y\).

Apply this with \(X=A\) and \(Y=J\):

\[
\operatorname{rank}(A+J)\le \operatorname{rank}(A)+1.
\]

Similarly,

\[
A=(A+J)-J,
\]

so

\[
\operatorname{rank}(A)\le \operatorname{rank}(A+J)+1.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\left|\operatorname{rank}(A+J)-\operatorname{rank}(A)\right|\le 1.
\]

The same argument applies to \(J-A\), since subtracting \(J\) is also a rank-one perturbation. Hence

\[
\left|\operatorname{rank}(J\pm A)-\operatorname{rank}(A)\right|\le 1
\]

for every square matrix \(A\) over every field.

The constant \(c=1\) is best possible, for example when \(A=0\):

\[
|\operatorname{rank}(J)-\operatorname{rank}(0)|=1.
\]

Thus the statement is true.

\[
\boxed{\text{True; one may take } c=1.}
\]
